pharm: Stimulates beta-2 adrenergic receptors on uterine smooth muscle, raising cyclic AMP to inhibit myometrial contractility and suppress premature labour
quick: IV infusion started ~50 micrograms/min, titrated; max ~350 micrograms/min
Used in pregnancy (>=22 weeks) as a tocolytic; not for use before 22 weeks
Used antenatally; not a chronic postpartum drug
Not applicable in the acute setting
Maternal/fetal heart rate, BP, ECG, fluid balance, glucose, potassium, lungs
summary: Ritodrine is a beta-2 adrenergic agonist formerly used as a tocolytic to suppress uncomplicated premature labour (generally after 22 weeks of gestation), most often given as a titrated intravenous infusion. It relaxes uterine smooth muscle by stimulating beta-2 receptors. Ritodrine has been WITHDRAWN from many markets (including the US, where it is no longer FDA-approved) because of serious maternal cardiovascular and metabolic adverse effects - notably pulmonary oedema, tachycardia, arrhythmia, myocardial ischaemia, hyperglycaemia and hypokalaemia - and limited evidence of improved neonatal outcomes. Where still available, it requires intensive maternal and fetal monitoring; many guidelines now prefer alternative tocolytics.
indications: Suppression of uncomplicated preterm labour (tocolysis), generally at or after 22 weeks of gestation, to allow time for corticosteroids and transfer to an appropriate unit

dosage.d: Start ~50 micrograms/min IV infusion, increase by ~50 micrograms/min every 10 minutes until contractions stop; usual effective 150-350 micrograms/min
dosage.t: Continuous IV, titrated to response and maternal heart rate
dosage.n: Do not exceed ~350 micrograms/min; keep maternal heart rate <120-140/min

dosage.d: Continue effective infusion rate for 12-48 h, then taper; oral maintenance (historically 10 mg) is no longer recommended
dosage.n: Total tocolysis usually limited to ~48 hours

admin: Administer as a controlled intravenous infusion via an infusion pump, ideally in a left-lateral position to reduce hypotension
Use the minimum effective rate and limit duration (typically up to 48 hours)
Restrict total fluid volume and use the most concentrated practicable solution to reduce the risk of pulmonary oedema
Continuously monitor maternal pulse, blood pressure, ECG, lung auscultation and fetal heart rate
Stop the infusion if maternal heart rate is persistently high, chest pain occurs, or signs of pulmonary oedema develop
Monitor blood glucose and potassium during infusion
moa: Ritodrine selectively stimulates beta-2 adrenergic receptors on uterine smooth muscle. Receptor activation raises intracellular cyclic AMP, which reduces intracellular calcium availability and inhibits actin-myosin interaction, decreasing the frequency and intensity of uterine contractions. Because beta-2 receptors are also present in the heart, blood vessels, bronchi and on metabolic pathways, ritodrine also causes tachycardia, peripheral vasodilation, bronchodilation, hyperglycaemia and hypokalaemia, which account for its adverse-effect profile.

absolute: Conditions where prolonging pregnancy is hazardous (e.g. eclampsia, severe pre-eclampsia, intrauterine death, chorioamnionitis, antepartum haemorrhage requiring delivery)
Maternal cardiac disease, arrhythmias or significant ischaemic heart disease
Hypersensitivity to ritodrine; gestation before about 22 weeks
relative: Concomitant corticosteroids (additive pulmonary oedema and metabolic effects)
Multiple pregnancy or fluid overload (increased pulmonary oedema risk)
monitor: Maternal heart rate, blood pressure and ECG

preg: Ritodrine is used during pregnancy specifically as a short-term tocolytic, generally only at or after 22 weeks of gestation; it is not used before viability and not for any non-obstetric indication. Use is balanced against significant maternal cardiovascular and metabolic risks, and treatment is limited to short courses under close monitoring.
lact: Ritodrine is an antenatal medication given to suppress labour and is not used chronically postpartum; routine breastfeeding data are limited and not clinically relevant to its intended short-term obstetric use.
renal: Use with caution in renal impairment because elimination may be reduced; monitor for accumulation and cardiovascular effects.
hepatic: Use with caution in hepatic impairment.

major: Beta-blockers - antagonise the tocolytic effect; avoid
Corticosteroids (often co-administered for fetal lung maturity) - increased risk of pulmonary oedema and metabolic disturbance
moderate: Drugs prolonging the QT interval / causing arrhythmia - additive risk
minor: Antidiabetic agents - may need adjustment due to hyperglycaemia
interactions.alcohol: Not applicable in the acute obstetric setting
interactions.diagnostics: Causes hyperglycaemia and hypokalaemia; monitor glucose and potassium during infusion

monitoring: Continuous maternal heart rate and blood pressure; ECG
Regular auscultation of the lungs for pulmonary oedema
Blood glucose and serum potassium during infusion
Strict fluid balance to avoid overload
counsel: This medicine is given by a drip to try to delay your labour for a short time
You may feel your heart racing, shakiness, flushing or nausea - tell the staff if these are severe
Report any chest pain or sudden breathlessness immediately
Your heart, blood pressure, breathing, your baby's heartbeat and your blood tests will be monitored closely
This drug has been withdrawn in many countries; your team will discuss alternatives if appropriate
pk: Uterine relaxation within minutes of starting the IV infusion
Steady-state plasma levels reached within about 1 hour of a constant infusion
Biphasic; terminal elimination half-life approximately 1.7-2.6 hours
Effect dependent on continued infusion; declines rapidly after stopping
Store as labelled at controlled room temperature; protect from light; prepare infusion freshly
pearls: WITHDRAWN in many markets and NOT FDA-approved - data from EMA/SmPC and BNF-type references
Major hazard is pulmonary oedema - restrict fluids, limit duration (~48 h) and watch the lungs
Causes maternal/fetal tachycardia, hyperglycaemia and hypokalaemia - monitor glucose and potassium
Contraindicated in maternal cardiac disease, eclampsia and conditions where delivery is needed
Many guidelines now prefer alternative tocolytics; use, if at all, with intensive monitoring
missed: Ritodrine is given as a clinician-controlled intravenous infusion in hospital for acute tocolysis, not as a patient-managed dose, so there is no missed-dose scenario.
overdose: Overdose produces exaggerated beta-agonist effects: severe tachycardia, palpitations, arrhythmia, hypotension, tremor, hyperglycaemia, hypokalaemia and pulmonary oedema. Stop the infusion immediately and provide supportive care; a cardioselective beta-blocker can be used cautiously to counteract severe cardiac effects, with correction of electrolytes and management of pulmonary oedema.
